claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 has a single-phase BCC state at high temperature.
Phase stability in high-temperature BCC Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by competition between a thermodynamic transformation driving force and diffusion-limited kinetics.
Al primarily induces a chemical-segregation or local-ordering tendency that destabilizes the homogeneous BCC matrix.
The BCC phase is not the most thermodynamically stable phase at lower temperatures.
Sluggish atomic diffusion in the multicomponent alloy suppresses transformation of BCC into ordered intermetallics or precipitate-containing states.
Al-induced local lattice distortions create kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion.
The complex energy landscape of the multicomponent alloy retards atomic mobility.
Sufficiently long thermal holds permit atomic reordering or segregation that is kinetically suppressed over shorter times.
Rapid cooling preserves a metastable BCC structure by limiting diffusion.
Rapidly quenched samples will largely retain the single-phase high-temperature BCC structure.
Slow or prolonged annealing below the high-temperature regime will produce secondary phases, precipitates, or compositional segregation.
The controlled comparison varies cooling rate or low-temperature annealing duration while holding composition, initial microstructure, and atmosphere constant.
The as-solidified or rapidly quenched single-phase BCC alloy serves as the baseline.
The hypothesis is restricted to conditions without stress-induced transformations, irradiation effects, or other non-thermal perturbations of diffusion.
The hypothesis applies in a temperature regime where atomic mobility is the dominant control on phase evolution.
XRD, TEM, and optionally atom-probe tomography can test for secondary phases, precipitates, and elemental partitioning after thermal treatment.
Failure of slow annealing or extended low-temperature dwell to produce detectable secondary phases or segregation relative to the quenched baseline would falsify the proposed mechanism.
